episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: What are we actually measuring?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down 31 motorcycles hit the road for fourth annual Cariboo Toy Run and LETTER: Williams Lake Lions Club raffle allows continued community support, plus 13 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Should arts and cultural organizations rely primarily on quantitative metrics like attendance counts to measure value and success, or should they prioritize qualitative community input and contextual understanding? Topics include: The distortion of metrics when counts become funding targets, Quantifiable versus unmeasurable value in journalism and cultural programming, How digital platforms' engagement metrics differ from analog measurement problems, Longevity and sustained presence as undervalued measures in annual grant cycles, Trust and familiarity as forms of accountability in small communities, Information design and how charts can legitimize questionable data, Participatory measurement: letting communities define what gets counted.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Williams Lake and District Seniors Activity Centre Society

discussion.central_question: Should arts and cultural organizations rely primarily on quantitative metrics like attendance counts to measure value and success, or should they prioritize qualitative community input and contextual understanding?
discussion.riley_position: Quantitative counts provide necessary, objective, and checkable baseline measures that funders and skeptics require to allocate resources fairly, though they should be supplemented with other inputs like subscriptions, editorial impact, and audience voices.
riley_key_evidence: A ticket count is 'the one number everybody can read the same way' and provides a floor for comparison across applications and years
Podcasts and web stories with repeat listener data show 'attention' better than one-off tickets
Raw audio of audience answers, published in full, creates an auditable record that 'the ones who care most' can verify
discussion.casey_position: Quantitative metrics become distorting ends rather than means, incentivizing organizations to optimize for countable outputs rather than meaningful community outcomes, and obscuring the actual value that emerges from sustained local presence and relationship.
casey_key_evidence: The Toy Run headline reported '31 motorcycles' while ignoring what toys did in living rooms; 'the number survives and the thing it was for drops out'
The Lancet study shows engagement metrics targeting young people's screen time led to documented health harms because dashboards 'counted time on screen, and time on screen became the goal'

A local paper's real value—watching officials and affecting policy—'produces no number at all' and 'a story that never gets written because an official knew someone was watching doesn't show up in anyone's analytics'
discussion.resolution: Riley and Casey agree counts will not disappear and disagree on whether they stay as a floor versus becoming a ceiling, but agree to pilot a Williams Lake experiment placing audience-generated questions alongside ticket counts on grant reports, with follow-up assessment of whether the audio answers change how organizations operate.
